title: RAG Revision Notes: From Ingestion to Cited Answers
summary: Quick revision notes on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, covering why RAG exists, then ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, prompt assembly and generation with citations. It ends with common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Why RAG and the Mental Model
points: RAG = retrieve relevant text at query time, put it in the prompt, and make the LLM answer from it. The model stays frozen; the knowledge lives outside it.
RAG fixes three LLM gaps: stale knowledge (training cutoff), private data it never saw, and hallucination with no source to check.
Two pipelines: offline indexing (ingest → chunk → embed → index) and online query (embed query → retrieve → rerank → assemble prompt → generate with citations).

RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context: RAG for fresh or private facts with citations; fine-tuning for style, format or behaviour; long context for a small, static corpus, but it costs more per query and recall drops in the middle.
Interview Point: Why not fine-tune the facts into the model? What are the two pipelines in RAG? When would you skip RAG and use long context?

chapters.title: Ingestion and Chunking
points: Ingestion: load sources (PDF, HTML, docs, DB rows), parse to clean text, strip boilerplate such as headers, footers and nav, and attach metadata (source, title, page, date, ACL) to every document.
Chunking splits documents into retrievable units. Chunks that are too big dilute the embedding; chunks that are too small lose context. A common start is 200-500 tokens with 10-20% overlap.

Strategies compared: fixed-size (fast, cuts mid-sentence), recursive by paragraph then sentence (good default), structure-aware by headings or code blocks (best for docs), semantic by embedding similarity (costly).
Example: split on headings, cap each chunk at 400 tokens, and prepend the section title to the chunk text so an orphan paragraph still carries its context.
Interview Point: How do you choose chunk size and overlap? Why keep metadata on each chunk? What breaks when you chunk tables or code with a fixed splitter?

chapters.title: Embeddings and Indexing
points: An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector so that similar meaning lands close together. Compare vectors with cosine similarity or dot product (equal on normalised vectors).
Use the same embedding model for chunks and queries. Changing the model means re-embedding the whole corpus. Check the model's max input tokens so chunks are not silently truncated.
Exact (flat) search compares against every vector: perfect recall but O(N). Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) trades a little recall for speed, using HNSW graphs or IVF clusters.

Vector store choices compared: pgvector (reuse existing Postgres), FAISS (library, in-memory), and managed or dedicated stores (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, OpenSearch) for scale and filtering. Store the chunk text and metadata beside the vector.
Interview Point: Why must query and chunk embeddings come from the same model? How does HNSW trade recall for speed? When is a flat index enough?

chapters.title: Retrieval and Reranking
points: Basic retrieval: embed the query, fetch the top-k nearest chunks (k is often 5-20), and apply a similarity threshold so weak matches are dropped rather than forced into the prompt.
Hybrid search combines dense vectors (meaning) with BM25 keywords (exact IDs, names, error codes). Merge the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank).
Rerank: retrieve wide (top 50) with a fast bi-encoder, then rescore with a cross-encoder that reads query and chunk together, and keep the top 5. This gives higher precision at higher latency.

Metadata filters (tenant, date, doc type, permissions) are applied at query time. Enforce ACL filters in retrieval so users never see chunks they should not. Query rewriting and HyDE help vague or multi-turn questions.
Interview Point: Why combine BM25 with vectors? What does a cross-encoder do that a bi-encoder cannot? How would you measure retrieval quality (recall@k, MRR)?

chapters.title: Prompt Assembly and Cited Generation
points: Prompt layout: system rules, then numbered context chunks each with a source ID, then the user question. Instruct the model to answer only from the context and to say "I don't know" if the context lacks the answer.

Context budget: top-k chunks must fit the window with room left for the answer. Dedupe near-identical chunks and order by relevance. Put the best chunks first and last, because middle chunks are recalled worst.

Citations: tag each chunk [1], [2] with its source and page, ask the model to cite IDs inline, then check that every cited ID exists in the retrieved set and map IDs back to links. Unverified citations are a failure.

Common mistakes: chunks too large or too small, no reranking, stuffing too much context, no refusal rule, not versioning the index, and never evaluating. Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) and generation (faithfulness, answer relevance) separately.
Interview Point: How do you stop the model from answering beyond the context? How do you verify citations? Where do you look first when answers are wrong, retrieval or generation?

chapters.title: RAG Cheat Sheet
points: Pipeline: ingest + metadata → chunk → embed → index (offline); embed query → hybrid retrieve → rerank → assemble prompt → generate + cite (online).
Defaults: chunk 200-500 tokens with 10-20% overlap; retrieve top 20-50, rerank to 5; same embedding model for index and query; cosine similarity; HNSW for scale.
Debug order for a bad answer: is the right chunk in the index? Is it in the top-k? Is it in the prompt? Does the answer follow the context? Fix the earliest failing stage.
Quality checklist: hybrid search, reranker, metadata and ACL filters, refusal instruction, verified citations, index versioning, and an eval set tracking recall@k and faithfulness.
Interview Point: Walk through RAG end to end in 60 seconds. What are the top three levers for better answers? How do you keep the index fresh when documents change?
